content: Health professionals play a critical role in the delivery of Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) services. Training curricula for these professionals must align with regulated scopes of practice and, at a minimum, introduce the essential components of VMMC and the service package to be provided. Key considerations for education include incorporating VMMC and other critical elements of adolescent-friendly and person-centered care into national pre-service training and continuing education requirements across relevant cadres. This involves both pre-service and continuing education institutions. Additionally, it is essential to establish competency requirements for all cadres of VMMC healthcare workers and develop national health education and training courses on adolescent health, including modules on interpersonal communication and patient safety in VMMC. Maintaining an efficient and effective health workforce requires robust management systems that address personnel recruitment, working conditions, and performance management, including monitoring and evaluation. A significant challenge for many countries is identifying and training the required number of personnel to achieve competence. Support and supervision should be person-centered, focusing on enhancing adolescent-friendly, integrated services. Key management, support, and supervision considerations include providing supportive supervision for adolescent-friendly and responsive care by healthcare workers offering VMMC services, integrating VMMC into national, district, and local structures for health-worker management, and implementing patient safety systems that enable learning from adverse events and include quality improvement measures. Health workforce planning should document and analyze the situation of health workers providing VMMC in light of strategic objectives. This includes projecting the number of clients, particularly adolescents, who will require VMMC services and developing systems to monitor skills distribution and retention. Broad incentive schemes may be necessary to ensure adequate staffing levels. Engaging community health workers and non-health actors, such as educators and community members, in community sensitization efforts can help sustain demand for VMMC services. Planning and facilitating the involvement of community health volunteers is also critical. Pre-service and continuing education should include VMMC in national training requirements and develop mechanisms to involve healthcare workers in determining their training and education needs. Competency-building activities should be conducted at national and district levels, including as part of recertification requirements. VMMC modules should be included in national adolescent health education and training courses, employing training methodologies that emphasize adolescent-friendly services and are both peopleand health worker-centered, such as blended learning approaches. Healthcare service delivery standards should be developed and implemented to assess adolescent-responsive VMMC services, patient safety, and infection prevention and control. VMMC programs should align with national systems of supportive supervision led by the Ministry of Health (MOH). To ensure the sustainability of VMMC services, country programs must transition from vertical and donor-dependent strategic information systems to integrated, country-owned systems for data collection and use. These systems should routinely collect data from the facility level through the national level. Key components for strategic information include developing efficient VMMC data collection methods that leverage electronic systems, reducing reliance on paper-based systems, and encouraging country-level data ownership. Data analysis and usage are critical for effective VMMC programming. A bottom-up approach to data analysis, starting at the facility level and moving to the program level, is essential. Countries, donors, and implementing partners must harmonize processes for VMMC data use. Key considerations include planning for data analysis and disaggregation by age and location, using data for reporting, planning, logistics management, evaluation, and quality assurance, and applying quality assurance policies to VMMC data. Safety monitoring systems for VMMC are crucial for detecting, reporting, and responding to adverse events related to circumcision procedures. Adverse events must be clearly defined, and the systems, structures, and resources required to address them must be well-described. Strategic information interventions should engage clinical staff more closely. A well-functioning health system ensures equitable access to essential medical products and technologies of assured quality, safety, and efficacy. Implementing sustainable VMMC services requires a durable logistics system, including commodity procurement, supply chain management, human resources, waste management, and proper storage. Accurate demand forecasts and timely ordering are crucial. National standards and guidelines are needed to ensure a continuous supply of quality VMMC supplies and equipment. Countries should consider VMMC when developing national plans for procuring surgical, obstetric, and anesthesia supplies. Key considerations include establishing national standards for the quality of VMMC supplies, guidelines on prescribing and dispensing practices, and strategies to support the rational use of supplies and equipment. Procurement and distribution systems for VMMC supplies should be integrated into centralized national systems. Supply chain costs must be considered when determining resource needs, and specific VMMC technologies, such as pre-qualified devices, should be strategically introduced and rolled out. Proper stock management practices at the facility level are essential to prevent expirations and stock-outs. Quality assurance processes and mechanisms are necessary to maintain or strengthen the quality of VMMC supplies and equipment. This includes facilitating access to safe, appropriate, and affordable male circumcision devices and addressing waste management requirements, such as segregation, storage, transport, treatment, and disposal of healthcare waste. Leadership and governance are critical for sustaining VMMC services. Synergies and efficiencies are enhanced when relevant sections of the MOH collaborate closely with implementing partners, communities, civil society, young people, and the private sector. A clear and agreed vision is needed to ensure leadership and governance structures address VMMC effectively. Accountability, oversight, and regulation mechanisms must be developed within the MOH to measure progress, identify challenges, and improve results. National programs should lead in coordinating, setting sustainability milestones, and revising regulations as needed. Key considerations include systems for support and supervision of VMMC led by the MOH, focal points or coordinators at various operational levels, and technical working groups for oversight and review of VMMC performance. Intersectoral coordination is crucial, involving collaboration with sectors such as education, culture, civil society, traditional/community leaders, youth, finance, and the private sector. Country leadership, ownership, and effective collaboration with partners are essential at all levels—national, district, and local.
